title: Senior Communications Officer
content:
JX Fund supports exiled media from countries where independent reporting is no longer possible due to repression, persecution, and censorship. It provides financial support through grants and complements this with tailored programs responding to the needs of exiled media. To this end, JX Fund collects and curates knowledge and data on the needs, challenges, and achievements of exiled media, conducts research, and connects and facilitates communication between various international actors. Its support programs are developed dynamically and in response to needs, based on the data and observations collected.

They are looking for a Senior Communications Officer to lead the JX Fund’s external communications across media, public audiences, policymakers, institutional donors and private philanthropists.

title: Program Coordinator, Eastern Europe/Central Asia
content:
The Program Coordinator is responsible for CPJ’s work in the region and leads research, documentation, and advocacy on press freedom violations. CPJ is seeking an individual with extensive experience covering press freedom issues in Russia and Eastern Europe, and an excellent understanding of the main challenges across the wider region. The candidate must be based in the ECA region and will be hired via an Employer of Record.

The Program Coordinator role requires a strong background in media, press freedom policy, and advocacy in the ECA region, excellent research and analysis skills, and the ability to work independently and proactively. The role also involves responding to journalist assistance cases, including support for journalists experiencing trauma or post-traumatic situations.

title: On Power, Truth, and Journalism
content:
In this conversation, Joseph Stiglitz, Nobel laureate and one of the world’s leading economists, reflects on the role of investigative journalism in holding power to account and informing the public.

He explores how economic and political systems shape access to information, why transparency is essential for democracy, and the challenges journalists face in making complex issues understandable and impactful.

Nobel Prize winner, Joseph Stiglitz, has been a regular speaker at GIJC. This video gathered some of his thoughts shared during the 2025 Global Investigative Journalism Conference

title: ‘Moving Just One Block in Port-Au-Prince Was Equivalent to Traveling Nearly 1,000km Elsewhere in the World’: The Challenges of Ethnographic Journalism in Haiti
content:
For over a decade, the Salvadoran journalist and anthropologist Juan José Martínez D’Aubuisson has used the practice of ethnographic journalism to explore violence and how gang-related crime has impacted communities across the Americas.

His reporting from Honduras, the Dominican Republic, and Haiti, to mention some of his most recent work, has won awards: In 2024, he received the Ortega y Gasset Award from El País for The Moskitia: The Honduran Jungle Drowning in Cocaine, a piece documenting the destruction of Central America’s largest rainforest by drug trafficking. That same year, Massacre Border, his investigation into the violence faced by Haitians in the Dominican Republic, was shortlisted for an award from the True Story Festival. In 2025, his investigation Searching for Mikelson: An Apartheid in the Caribbean won the prestigious Gabo Award in the text category.

title: Israel’s Occupation of Southern Lebanon, The US$1 Trillion Pentagon Budget, How Amazon’s AI Eats Rare Books, Tracing Britain’s DNA History
content:
Israel’s military campaign in southern Lebanon has displaced more than one million people and destroyed thousands of homes. Using satellite imagery analysis, a Financial Times investigation examined the widespread destruction that has occurred before and after an initial ceasefire in April. Our latest Top 10 in Data Journalism round-up, looking at stories from August 12 to 25, also includes a piece from The Economist comparing how school-aged children perform when using AI, a Bellingcat investigation following the journey of a Russian-sanctioned ship from the Sea of Japan to the west of Africa, and a ProPublica analysis of the unprecedented Pentagon military spending on programs that are increasingly expensive and delayed.

title: This Nonprofit-Based Data App Could Change How You Cover Wildfires
content:
If you are an environmental journalist in the US West, covering wildfires may be a common chore. Watch Duty is a data app that will rescue you.

Not always “data” data, it is still a fire hose of critical information. It will repay your efforts to discover it. SEJournal has, over the years, offered many resources for covering wildfires. But we neglected this one. It is one of the best. Start exploring it here.

Watch Duty is a nongovernmental nonprofit staffed by experienced disaster professionals, tech professionals, and volunteers. It is funded by paid memberships and grants. You can get the basic info for free. It has a huge user base and gets massive online traffic.

If someone in your audience (or you) owns a cozy hideaway in some mountain forest, you need it — because government notification systems don’t always work. Toolbox observes that US President Donald Trump is reorganizing federal wildfire response. Hideaway owners may want to pay the US$24.99 for a yearly membership.

And you can get it on your smartphone as you are racing toward the fire. Or away from it.

title: GIJN Masterclass Round-Up: Key Investigative Topics
content:
GIJN’s Global Academy is your gateway to investigative journalism training. Through masterclass videos, training programs (in person or online), webinars, or mentorship programs, the Academy helps journalists at every stage strengthen their investigative skills, connect with peers, and continue learning. In this post, we’ve gathered some of our recent expert masterclass videos covering a wide range of critical investigative topics, from food insecurity to exposing corruption to leak-based exposés.

In this masterclass video, Thin Lei Win, lead reporter at Lighthouse Reports, shares four key lessons for investigating hunger and the global food system.

She explains how to define food insecurity beyond availability, including access, use, and stability, and how to find and verify reliable data through sources like FAOSTAT and the World Resources Institute. Thin also urges journalists to map the whole value chain, from farmers to corporations, to expose inequalities, and to center communities and their actions, telling stories with people, not just about them.

title: New York Times’s Malachy Browne on the Future of Visual Investigations in the Age of AI
content:
When Malachy Browne started piecing together videos of the Arab Spring in early 2011, he wasn’t thinking about building a new kind of journalism. He was just trying to figure out what was real.

What began as the niche practice of verifying shaky mobile phone footage in an era of social media chaos has since become one of the most consequential developments in modern journalism.

As a co-founder of The New York Times’ visual investigations team, Browne helped pioneer a form of reporting that combines traditional investigative techniques with digital forensics. He uses satellite imagery, geolocation, and video analysis to uncover war crimes, expose abuses of power, and establish the facts of contested events.

The idea for the team emerged gradually. Browne credits early inspiration to groups such as Forensic Architecture, SITU Research, and Bellingcat. A turning point came at a gathering of investigators and technologists at Carnegie Mellon University, where researchers demonstrated new ways of documenting war crimes.

creator: Maurice Oniang'o

title: How Many Tobacco Shops Are Near Your Town’s Schools? Using Georeferenced Data Analysis for Location-Based Investigations
content:
Have you ever wondered what it would look like to have a list of every hospital in a city and map how close, or how far, they sit from vulnerable communities? Or to check whether there’s a correlation between gas stations, bars, and liquor distributors? Or whether poor neighborhoods have the same ratio of healthcare facilities, police stations, fire departments, and schools as wealthier ones? No single list can answer questions like these, but there is a workable method for building the databases and maps that can.

Every journalistic investigation starts with a good question, and a good question is rarely answered by a single source. The Map of Tobacco Shops project, produced by O Joio e O Trigo and funded by ACT Health Promotion, in which we identified more than 1,500 tobacco retailers within 100 meters of schools across Brazil, began with exactly that kind of question. This article walks through the process that connected our starting point to the answers we eventually found.

title: ‘Investigative Journalism Goes Beyond Numbers:’ Reporting on Health and the Environment in Côte d’Ivoire
content:
Marthe Akissi Kra is a familiar voice on Côte d’Ivoire’s public broadcaster Radiodiffusion Télévision Ivoirienne (RTI), where she reports on environmental conservation, sustainable development, health, and community affairs in the West African country.

She spends much of her time in the field reporting on the effects of climate change in Côte d’Ivoire and for Ivorians, such as the pressures facing protected areas — gold mining, population growth, the loss of its rainforests, poaching — and the environmental and health implications for local communities on the frontlines.

Kra has won several regional and international awards for her work, including the Media for Science and Development Award’s Super Prize for science journalism (Cote d’Ivoire), the second Norbert Zongo African Investigative Journalism Prize (PAJI-NZ) in the radio category, and the 2022 Prix Eco-Reportages du club de la presse Drôme-Ardèche (France). She was also recently selected Country Coordinator for the Network of Science Journalists for Francophone Africa (RSAF-Côte d’Ivoire).

title: GIJN Masterclass Round-Up: Artificial Intelligence
content:
GIJN’s Global Academy is your gateway to investigative journalism training. Through masterclass videos, training programs (in person or online), webinars or mentorship programs, the Academy helps journalists at every stage strengthen their investigative skills, connect with peers, and continue learning. In this post, we’ve gathered some of our recent expert masterclass videos that tackle different aspects of investigating AI as well as responsibly and ethically using it in your reporting.

In this masterclass video, Gabriel Geiger, investigative journalist at Lighthouse Reports, shares practical tips for reporting on how governments use algorithms and AI systems in public services such as policing, welfare, and healthcare.

Geiger explains how reporters can start investigating these systems by identifying government processes that may rely on automation, such as benefits decisions or risk assessments. Key reporting strategies include requesting documents and data about the systems, filing targeted freedom-of-information requests, and building sources inside institutions that interact with the technology.

title: Investigating Technology and AI in Conflict
content:
Reporting on modern warfare no longer relies solely on focusing on what is happening on the front line. Journalists must also show how the technologies and AI systems increasingly shaping conflict are conceived, financed and coded in conference rooms, data centres and technology offices far from the battlefield.

In this emerging military-technological complex, a new phase of the military-industrial complex, cloud platforms, AI models, and commercial infrastructure have become integral to the conduct of war. Yet this weaponization of technology makes accountability harder to trace than ever.

War reporters need more than flak jackets and nerves of steel. They must also dig into procurement records, trade databases, export licenses, corporate filings, and the digital breadcrumbs left behind by the military-tech ecosystem to understand complicity and responsibility in conflict.

In this workshop, based on an upcoming GIJN reporting guide, Dr. Iain Overton will introduce a practical framework for investigating the technological systems behind modern warfare, from surveillance infrastructure and automated decision-making to the financial flows that make them possible.

title: 10 Practical Tips for Verifying Scientific Claims
content:
A paper published in a scientific journal can seem like a promising lead for a news story or the beginning of an investigation. Yet peer review does not involve repeating every experiment or verifying every piece of data. Research may contain methodological flaws or unintentional errors; sometimes, the data have been manipulated or fabricated.

In 2025, journalist Frederik Joelving and computer scientists Cyril Labbé and Guillaume Cabanac published the findings of a six-month investigation into so-called scientific paper mills. These paper mills are businesses that produce and sell fraudulent scientific papers, often using fabricated or manipulated data.

Among the cases they examined was one in which a paper was first questioned by cancer researchers Soren Zielske and Danny Welch. The two scientists had tried to build on its findings but could not reproduce the results. Looking more closely, they found identical data in graphs that were supposed to represent different experiments. In 2020, Zielske posted his concerns on PubPeer and contacted the journal’s editor. The paper was later retracted for “falsified materials and/or data.”

title: Spain’s Solar Eclipses, Russia-Ukraine Drone Warfare, ICE Detention Camp Overcrowding, and Tracking the Spread of Fake News
content: As large swaths of Europe and parts of North America and Africa prepared for a solar eclipse this week, news outlets sought to capture the rare astronomical event that many people may never see again in their lifetime. El Orden Mundial’s visual story explored why Spain is one of the exceptions, with the country set to experience two more eclipses within two years. Our roundup of the Top 10 in Data journalism, looking at stories from July 23 to August 11, also includes a Reuters graphical illustration showing how drones are transforming fighting on the frontlines in Ukraine, an ARIJ investigation examining civilian-to-combatant casualty ratios in the Middle East under different US presidents, and a Straits Times analysis modeling how early debunking can stop the spread of misinformation.

title: Investigating Inside Conflict Zones and Areas Controlled by Armed Groups: Lessons from South Asia and the Middle East
content:
In October 2021, journalist Shahid Zehri was driving home to Karachi through the town of Hub, in Pakistan’s Balochistan province, when a bomb planted under his car seat detonated. He died of his injuries hours later.

The Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), a separatist rebel group regarded as a terrorist organization by the Pakistani government and several other countries, including the United States, claimed responsibility, accusing Zehri of spying for Pakistan’s security forces, without offering evidence. “It is intolerable that separatist rebels are able, with impunity, to claim the right to kill journalists in a completely arbitrary manner,” Reporters Without Borders (RSF) spokesperson Pauline Adès-Mével said in a statement in response to the killing.

title: Silencing Journalists Online: How Copyright Is Being Weaponized Against Investigative Journalists
content:
A new form of censorship is emerging globally to silence the work of journalists and activists. On digital platforms like Facebook or Google, journalists’ social media accounts and their stories are being targeted with fake complaints aimed at silencing their work online.

The perpetrators are often shady firms hired by powerful interests who offer to remove content their clients don’t like online by playing with digital platforms rules.

Reputation cleaning firms or individuals make up false claims of copyright infringement and pressure the digital platforms to take down targeted contents. Do they succeed? Often, they do.  And Big Tech companies sometimes even refuse to disclose information on who makes these complaints.

The mechanics are straightforward and hard to fight: scammers duplicate the journalists’ social media accounts or content and file fake copyright infringement claims to digital platforms, accusing the journalists of impersonating them thus violating the platforms’ rules. This results in the journalists’ accounts or posts being suspended or banned, with the victims sometimes not being aware of the reasons they’re kicked out.

title: Strategies To Seek Funding For Investigative Journalism
content:
We are in a challenging environment for investigative journalism. The need for investigative reporting exceeds reliable funding sources for it in many parts of the world. Nonetheless, investigative journalists are approaching the challenges with creativity and resilience, and have multiple paths to explore to seek funding. This session will provide a kind of decision tree or logic to help journalists determine what paths may be worth exploring to find story and project funding in their region or topic. Our talk is aimed at individual journalists who have not done fundraising for their work and are seeking advice on where to get started. We’ll explore key considerations and pathways you can choose depending on your circumstances to explore funding options and pursue those that may fit for you and support the journalism you seek to produce.

This session will not provide suggestions or lists of specific funding sources.  Funding options vary greatly by country, region and even your own individual situations. However, a tip sheet will provide links to global organizations that can help you research grant options, examples of journalism networks and networked funders and some other tips.

title: GIJN Masterclass Round-Up: Data Journalism
content:
GIJN’s Global Academy is your gateway to investigative journalism training. Through masterclass videos, training programs (in person or online), webinars or mentorship programs, the Academy helps journalists at every stage strengthen their investigative skills, connect with peers, and continue learning. In this post, we’ve gathered some of our recent expert masterclass videos that tackle different aspects of using data in your investigations.

In this masterclass video, Fabiola Torres, founder and director of Salud con Lupa, shares a practical approach to data journalism, starting not with tools, but with documents.

She explains how investigations often begin with access to information requests, and how journalists must build their own datasets from messy, fragmented sources like PDFs. Using simple tools like spreadsheets and keyword searches, she shows how to organize, analyze, and extract insights from large volumes of information.

This grounded, hands-on guide cuts through the hype to help: master the basics, trust your reporting instincts, and turn raw data into impactful investigations.

title: Can We Gamify That? The Innovators Turning Investigations on Spying Scandals and Vote Rigging into Video Games
content:
An animated phone vibrates on a blackened screen as ominous piano music tinkles in the background. When you click, speech bubbles appear. “It’s Thanasis Koukakis,” the person on the other end says. “I’m borrowing a phone… Just don’t try to reach out to me for now. Texts, calls, try to avoid it.”

This is the opening scene of “Predatorgate,” a new video game based on an investigation into the Predator spyware scandal in Greece. Koukakis was the reporter at the heart of that real-life story who discovered his phone had been infected with the highly invasive spyware. This narrative game is based on the investigation by Inside Story, and shows what it’s like to be in the shoes of a journalist under threat of illegal surveillance. In the game — which takes an estimated 30 minutes to play — Koukakis is a colleague who discovers his phone has been targeted.
